Welcome to this journey where grief and identity are woven together in the most unexpected places—like the bustling aisles of a Korean grocery store. Imagine stepping into a world where every ingredient, every scent, and every shared meal carries the echo of memory and longing. That’s the heart of Michelle Zauner’s remarkable story, Crying in H Mart, where food isn’t just sustenance—it’s a portal to family, heritage, and the ache of losing someone you love.
Together, we’ll explore how the comfort of tradition gently meets the sharpness of loss, and how every ritual—every recipe—becomes a bridge to the past and a lifeline for the future. As we move through the flavors and textures of Korean cuisine, you’ll find they’re so much more than just dishes on a table. They’re the warmth of home, the bittersweet tug of change, and the way we keep our loved ones close, even when they’re gone.
Along the way, we’ll navigate what it means to grow up between cultures—the push and pull between fitting in and staying true to yourself. We’ll see how love can be shown in the smallest acts of care, sometimes unspoken, but always deeply felt. The story isn’t just about mourning; it’s about resilience, connection, and discovering who we are through what we remember, what we share, and what we carry forward.
So, let’s step into this world together. Let’s open ourselves to the beauty and pain of holding on, letting go, and finding our place within the enduring bonds of food, memory, and love.

Chapter One: Grocery Store Aisles and the Weight of Memory
You know, there’s a certain ache that creeps in when you least expect it. Maybe for you, it’s a song that drifts through the car speakers, or a street corner that brings back a wave of nostalgia. But for some, it’s the bright, humming aisles of a grocery store—where the scent of ripe fruit and the neat rows of packages suddenly open a portal to another life.
Imagine this: Standing in the heart of a bustling Asian supermarket, a young woman is surrounded by shelves lined with dried seaweed, jars of fermented vegetables, and the gentle chatter of shoppers speaking a language she only half understands. Every item she passes seems to carry the weight of memory, each one a quiet reminder of a mother who’s no longer there.
Isn’t it easy to forget how food can become its own language? Especially when you’re growing up between two cultures. For kids of immigrants, the kitchen isn’t just a place to eat—it’s the very first classroom. The dinner table? That’s where love gets measured, not in words, but in spoonfuls and side dishes. A mother’s hands are always moving—chopping, stirring, tasting, and quietly showing the way. The lessons are never formal: rinse the rice until the water runs clear, trust your nose to pick the sweetest melon, fold the dumplings just so, so they won’t burst in the pot. These everyday rituals turn into a kind of inheritance, passed down with every repetition and gentle correction.
But here’s something to pay attention to. When loss arrives, it doesn’t just take the person you loved. It pulls loose all the threads that held your sense of self together. Suddenly, the grocery store—a place you’ve visited a hundred times—becomes a test. Which brand of soy sauce did she always reach for? How did she get the broth to taste just right? The answers feel lost in the past, and every time you try to recreate a favorite dish, there’s that fear: What if I get it wrong?
In those moments, grief stops being just a feeling. It settles in your chest, a tightness that lingers, even after the tears have faded. The world keeps spinning, but time seems to slow down right there in the aisles of H Mart—where what’s familiar and what’s foreign seem to collide. The longing for connection is as real as the smell of kimchi, and finding comfort turns into a journey through memory, culture, and all the complicated love between a mother and her child.
Most people don’t realize just how much of who we are is built on those small, everyday rituals with family. And for those who grow up straddling two worlds, those rituals are the only bridge to a heritage that’s both distant and deeply important. Losing a parent makes that bridge feel almost impossibly fragile. But holding onto those traditions—no matter how shaky it feels—is really just another way of holding onto yourself.

Chapter 2: Growing Up Between Worlds—Family, Culture, and the Search for Belonging
You know, childhood is never quite as straightforward as we might hope. But just imagine what it’s like when you’re growing up between two worlds—caught in that space where cultures meet, and sometimes, collide.
Picture a small town, the kind where everyone seems to know everyone else. Now, think of a young girl who stands out simply because her family’s different. At home, there’s a mother who’s sharp, quick with a joke, but also holds her daughter to high standards. She’s a comfort and, honestly, sometimes a puzzle. The rules at home? They’re strict. The food? Well, it’s delicious, but it doesn’t look anything like what her classmates bring for lunch. And at their dinner table, the conversation is sprinkled with words that you just can’t find in any English dictionary.
Then there’s school—a whole different universe. The pressure to fit in is everywhere. And when you’re one of the few Asian faces in the room, you can’t really blend in, no matter how much you might want to. Those homemade lunches draw curious looks, sometimes even awkward jokes. So, what do you do? You learn to hide little pieces of yourself. Maybe you laugh along, or brush off a comment. But deep down, it can feel lonely—like you’re invisible in all the ways that matter.
Back at home, things aren’t always easier. The relationship with her mom is complicated. There’s love there, for sure, but it often comes wrapped in criticism and sky-high expectations. Praise is rare, and hugs? Not so much. Instead, affection shows up in everyday acts—like making your favorite meal or fixing your jacket before you head out. The mom’s hopes and worries come from her own journey as an immigrant. She wants her daughter to succeed, to stay connected to her roots, and there’s always that underlying fear of losing her to a world she doesn’t fully understand. The daughter feels the weight of those expectations. Sometimes she resents them, but, more than anything, she just wants her mom’s approval.
Food becomes both the battleground and the bridge between them. The mother insists on traditional recipes, explaining why each ingredient matters and sharing stories of her childhood. The daughter, meanwhile, sometimes just wants pizza or a burger—something easy, something that won’t stand out at the lunch table. But there’s comfort in those familiar flavors from home. Eventually, she realizes these meals are more than just food—they’re a way to keep her mother’s culture alive, a way of saying “I love you,” even if the words aren’t spoken out loud.
As the daughter grows into adolescence, the gap between mother and daughter starts to widen. She pushes back, looking for a bit of freedom, some independence. Fights break out over grades, friends, and plans for the future. The mother’s worries sound a lot like control, while the daughter’s need for space comes off as ungrateful. But really, both are just scared of losing each other—afraid that if they drift apart, they might not find their way back.
If you’ve grown up in an immigrant family, you probably know this feeling—the constant balancing act between honoring where you’ve come from and figuring out where you’re headed next. It’s a dance that never really ends; a push and pull between belonging and becoming yourself.
But here’s what matters most: it’s those quiet, everyday moments—the shared meals, the little acts of care, that silent understanding—that remind us love is always there, even when it’s complicated.

Chapter 3: Illness, Caregiving, and the Fragility of Connection
Life can change in an instant, can’t it? One moment, everything feels predictable—then something happens that turns it all upside down.
When a parent falls ill, the entire family dynamic shifts. Suddenly, that daughter who once clashed with her mom’s rules is the one guiding her mother through hospital corridors, trying to make sense of medical terms that seem to multiply every day. The certainty of childhood? It fades, replaced by the unpredictability of illness—and every single day becomes a test of endurance, and hope.
The diagnosis—well, it always feels like a shock. It’s a stark reminder that even the strongest people we know are still so vulnerable. The mom who used to be full of life and energy now struggles against exhaustion from treatments and pain. And the daughter? She’s suddenly a caregiver, juggling her own needs with the ever-growing demands of her family. There are moments of real frustration, times when it all just feels overwhelming. But there are also those unexpected moments of tenderness—the quiet comfort of a gentle touch, laughter that bubbles up even when things look bleak, or simply sitting together in silence, sharing a kind of intimacy that wasn’t there before.
Food starts to mean something different during times like these. The daughter throws herself into finding the perfect meals to tempt her mom’s fading appetite. She sifts through cookbooks, calls relatives for recipes, and pours her love into every dish she prepares. Each meal becomes a way to fight back against the illness—a small gesture of hope, a way to stay connected. The kitchen transforms into a sanctuary, a place where she can actually do something that matters, even when so much feels out of her control.
Caregiving is strange that way—it can feel incredibly isolating, but it also brings people closer together. Friends and extended family pitch in when they can, but most of the responsibility falls on those who are closest. The daughter learns how to navigate the healthcare maze, advocate for her mom, and somehow find little moments of grace in all the chaos. There are setbacks, sure—and disappointments. Yet there are also moments of closeness: a shared story, a favorite song playing softly in the background, or a quiet talk in the middle of the night.
As the illness progresses, the daughter can’t ignore the reality of loss. That fear of saying goodbye is always there. But so is the drive to make every remaining moment count. The routines of care—prepping meals, giving medicine, sitting by the bedside—become their own kind of ritual. They’re ways of holding onto the relationship, of honoring a bond that’s shaped her whole life.
Most people don’t realize just how much strength it takes to care for someone who’s dying. It’s exhausting, physically and emotionally. But it’s also one of the most profound acts of love there is.
In the end, what really matters are the small acts of kindness—the willingness to show up, day after day. Those are the moments that last.

Chapter 4: Grief, Food, and the Search for Meaning.
When loss finally shows up in our lives, it’s strange—it’s something you know is coming, but you’re never really ready. Suddenly, everything feels emptier, a little quieter, as if something vital has been pulled away from the world you know.
For a daughter, grief isn’t just one feeling—it’s like walking through a landscape that’s always changing. Sometimes it hits hard and fast, almost unbearable. Other times, it just lingers, dull but always there. And the absence of her mother is everywhere, but nowhere more than in the kitchen. The routines of cooking that used to bring comfort now feel almost echoing and hollow.
After the loss, she finds herself turning to food as a way to cope. Think about it—she starts searching for the dishes her mom used to make, chasing after those familiar flavors and textures that defined her childhood. It’s bittersweet. Each meal is a comfort, but also a reminder of what’s no longer there. Yet, in every recipe, there’s a piece of her mother’s memory—a way to say goodbye and to hold on, both at once.
Cooking becomes something more than just making meals—it turns into therapy. She tries out new recipes, reaches out to relatives for those old family secrets, and really digs into the traditions of her mother’s culture. She starts to realize that food is so much more than fuel. It’s a way to connect to the past, to honor those who came before, and to look for meaning even when things feel lost.
Grief can feel incredibly lonely, but here’s something interesting—it can actually bring people together. The daughter finds solace in sharing meals with friends and family, swapping stories, and remembering the good times. She discovers she’s not alone; others have been through this too. And the simple act of gathering around a table becomes a powerful way to heal. The kitchen, once filled with sadness, slowly transforms into a place of warmth and renewal.
With time, she learns something important: grief isn’t really something you “get over.” Instead, it becomes part of who you are. The pain may never totally disappear, but it settles in, woven into the story of your life—a reminder of the love that shaped you. Through food, through memories, and with the support of others, she finds a way forward, carrying her mother’s legacy every step of the way.
Most of us don’t realize just how much healing can happen over a simple meal. Food has this incredible power—to bring us together, to bridge the distance between what was and what is, and to offer comfort during even the hardest times. In the end, it’s these small moments of connection that help us navigate grief and find our way back to hope.

Chapter 5: Reclaiming Heritage and Forging a New Identity.
When the initial shock of loss finally starts to fade, what’s left behind is this slow, uneven path of rebuilding. Picture the daughter—standing at a crossroads, unsure, grieving, and trying to figure out who she is now. There are setbacks. Doubts sneak in. She finds herself wondering: how do you honor your mother’s memory, while also carving out your own story? It’s even trickier being the child of immigrants, isn’t it? You’re caught in between—never fully fitting in here or there.
So, what does she do? She dives headfirst into her mother’s culture. She starts learning the language, tasting the foods that once felt unfamiliar, even traveling back to her mother’s homeland. It’s both thrilling and a little scary. There are moments when she’s acutely aware of what’s been lost—but also moments of discovery. She realizes, reclaiming her heritage isn’t about getting it perfect. It’s about showing up, making the effort, and being willing to stumble along the way.
And then, there’s art. Creative expression becomes her lifeline. She pours her emotions into music, into her writing, into anything that lets her make sense of what she’s feeling. Through creativity, she finds a way to process her grief, to pull meaning out of the chaos, and—maybe most importantly—to connect with others who know exactly what she’s going through.
This journey of self-discovery? It’s messy. Sometimes, she feels clear and strong. Other times, she’s lost all over again. But slowly, she learns to embrace the complexity of her identity. She starts to celebrate the parts of herself shaped by her mother’s culture, and she finds a quiet pride in her heritage. She also gives herself permission to fall short sometimes, knowing that becoming who you are is a lifelong process.
Most people don’t see how brave you have to be to claim a heritage that’s always felt just out of reach. It’s rarely neat or easy, but it’s so worth it. In the end, she doesn’t find belonging by picking one culture over another. She finds it by cherishing the richness and the complexity of her own story.

Chapter 6: The Unspoken Language of Mothers and Daughters
You know, sometimes the deepest conversations don’t need any words at all. It’s that quick glance across a crowded room, or two hands reaching for the same ingredient in the kitchen. Even a single sigh can say so much, can’t it?
After her mother passed away, the daughter found herself replaying these silent exchanges over and over, almost like she was trying to read between the lines of her own memories. She started to realize just how much was shared in those pauses, in the way a gesture or a look could fill a whole afternoon with meaning. And honestly, the ache of missing someone is often sharpest in those quiet moments, when you notice what’s missing—not the words, but the spaces between them.
She can still picture her mother standing behind her at the stove, gently correcting her grip on a knife or nudging her to taste the broth one more time. There wasn’t a lot of praise, but there was always attention—a kind of steady watchfulness that shaped how she saw herself. Now, in her own quiet kitchen, the daughter tries to mimic those movements, almost like she’s hoping to bring back that sense of belonging. And sometimes, she catches her own reflection scolding her, using the same impatient but caring tone her mother once did.
It hits her just how much of their relationship lived in what went unsaid. She remembers the frustration of never quite measuring up, always longing for approval that seemed just out of reach. But in the wake of loss, she starts to see those moments through new eyes. The criticism, the high standards, the insistence on tradition—they were all ways her mother showed love, even if they were filtered through a different culture, a different time.
Most of us never really notice how much is carried in a simple gesture or a sigh. But now, the daughter learns to watch herself, to recognize all those little ways she’s internalized her mother’s lessons. She finds herself reaching for the same brands at the grocery store, folding laundry with the same precision, even humming the same old songs. And in these tiny acts, she feels her mother close—a gentle reminder that she’s never truly alone.
Understanding all of this isn’t quick or easy. It comes in fits and starts. Some days, she feels angry—burdened by expectations she didn’t ask for. But other days, she feels grateful, aware of the strength and resilience that have been passed down to her.
The unspoken language between mothers and daughters? It’s complicated, no doubt about it. But it’s also enduring—a quiet thread that ties them together, no matter how much time or distance lies between them.

Chapter 7. Music, Memory, and the Art of Holding On.
You know, sometimes the things that save us are the ones we never see coming. For the daughter, it’s music. It becomes her lifeline—a way to work through her grief, to hold onto memories, and slowly, to heal. She pours every ounce of sorrow and longing into her art. Creating music isn’t just something she does... it’s how she survives, how she tries to make sense of a world that suddenly feels unfamiliar.
There are nights when she’s alone, just her and her instrument. She lets the music transport her back to childhood. She can almost hear her mother’s laughter, feel the rhythm of their old routines, and sense the comfort of a favorite melody drifting through their house. Each song she plays becomes a memory—a gentle way of holding onto the past, even as she tries to move forward.
What’s interesting is, her music doesn’t stay private for long. Out in the world, people start to notice. Listeners reach out and share their own stories—their own losses and longings. Suddenly, the daughter realizes she’s not alone. There’s a whole community of people who understand what it means to lose a parent, to search for meaning after loss. Sharing her art turns into something bigger—a way to connect, to build bridges across the empty spaces grief leaves behind.
Most folks don’t realize just how powerful creative expression can be when you’re dealing with grief. For the daughter, music isn’t just an escape—it’s a way to honor her mother’s memory. Every time she performs, it’s a tribute. It’s a reminder that love doesn’t just disappear; it endures, even after someone’s gone. Through her music, she finds purpose—a reason to keep going, even on the hard days.
Of course, it’s not always easy. There are moments when doubt creeps in, when the pain feels way too raw to turn into words or melodies. But then, there are moments of clarity—times when the music flows effortlessly, and she can almost feel her mother sitting right there beside her. And in those moments, she realizes something important: healing isn’t about forgetting. It’s about discovering new ways to remember.

Chapter 8: The Messiness of Healing and the Work of Forgiveness
Healing isn’t a neat, tidy process. If you’ve ever tried to move through pain or loss, you know what I mean—it’s more like a winding, unpredictable journey, full of twists, turns, and unexpected stops.
That’s exactly what the daughter in this story discovers. She’s stumbling through the aftermath of losing her mother, completely unsure of the way forward. Some days, she wakes up feeling strong, ready to take on the world.
But then there are those other days—when even getting out of bed feels impossible.
Regret starts to creep in. She thinks about all the things she never said, the apologies she never made, and those moments of anger that, looking back now, just seem so small.
The guilt? It’s heavy. It presses down on her in ways she never expected. She can’t help but wonder—could she have done more? Should she have been more patient? More understanding? Maybe just… more present?
But these questions don’t have simple answers. And forgiveness—especially forgiving yourself—takes real time.
What she learns, slowly, is that healing isn’t about wiping the slate clean or pretending the past never happened. It’s really about learning to carry those memories, to live with them, and to make peace with her own imperfections.
She starts to realize that both she and her mom did the best they could, with what they knew at the time. Little by little, she forgives herself for the moments she fell short. And she forgives her mother, too—for the times she was tough to love.
Most people don’t realize just how much bravery it takes to walk through grief. The daughter comes to see that healing isn’t a finish line you cross—it’s a practice.
It’s about showing up each day, even when it’s hard. About letting yourself feel the pain, and letting go of what you can’t change. There aren’t any shortcuts here. No quick fixes.
It’s just the steady, quiet work of putting one foot in front of the other.
And over time, she starts to find moments of peace. She learns to celebrate the good memories, to honor the tough ones, and to accept that both are part of her story.
The process isn’t over—and maybe it never will be. But she begins to trust herself, knowing that, step by step, she’ll find her way.

Chapter 9. Community, Ritual, and the Power of Shared Experience.
No one really faces grief all by themselves. The daughter comes to realize this as she starts reaching out—to friends, to family, and even to strangers who’ve walked a similar road. She finds comfort in simple rituals of remembrance—maybe lighting a candle, sharing a meal, or telling stories that stretch late into the night.
These small acts become her way of keeping her mother’s memory close, almost weaving her loss right into the fabric of her everyday life.
There are gatherings where laughter mixes with tears, where the pain of missing someone gets just a bit softer, simply because others are there too.
She learns that grief isn’t just a private sorrow—it’s something shared. By opening up about her story, she invites others to share theirs. And together, they discover a quiet strength in being vulnerable, in letting those walls down for a little while.
Food stays at the heart of these rituals. The daughter begins to host dinners, cooking her mother’s recipes for friends and family.
Each dish tells a story—it’s a conversation, a way to pass down traditions and build new memories at the same table. The kitchen turns into a place of healing, where love is measured in second helpings and the warmth of shared meals.
Most of us don’t realize just how much comfort there is in simply being with others. Community, she learns, isn’t only about support—it’s about connection. It’s that gentle reminder that none of us are really alone in our struggles.
Over time, the rituals of grief shift. They become rituals of renewal, helping her move forward without ever leaving the past behind.
As the years pass, the daughter feels a pull toward new communities—children of immigrants, fellow artists, others who are mourning too. She discovers there’s something powerful about coming together, about sharing food and stories.
It turns out, that’s the true antidote to loneliness.
And in those moments, she feels her mother’s presence most deeply—a quiet reassurance that love, in all its forms, truly endures.

Chapter 10: Carrying the Legacy Forward.
As time goes by, you know, the sharp sting of grief starts to soften around the edges. The daughter finds herself looking ahead, wondering—how can she carry her mother’s legacy forward? It’s not just about remembering. It’s about living in a way that truly honors what’s been lost.
She keeps cooking, creating, and connecting with others. The lessons her mother shared—about food, about family, about being resilient—these become the foundation of her life now. She passes them along, too. Teaching friends how to make kimchi, writing songs that capture the messy beauty of love and loss, and reaching out to comfort those who are struggling.
Here’s something to really think about: legacy isn’t just what’s left behind. It’s in the choices we make, every single day. The daughter learns to celebrate her heritage, leaning into the parts of herself that once felt strange or even uncomfortable. Now, she finds pride in her story—realizing it’s both one-of-a-kind and something many people can relate to.
Most people don’t realize how powerful the little acts of remembrance can be. The daughter discovers that honoring her mom isn’t about grand gestures. It’s about living with intention and kindness. Every meal she cooks, every song she writes, every caring act—each is a quiet way of saying, “I remember you. I carry you with me.”
This journey isn’t over, but she doesn’t feel lost anymore. She’s learned to live with her grief, to find meaning in life’s messiness, and to carry her mother’s love forward into the world.

As we wrap up, I want you to remember—grief isn’t some neat or predictable process. If you’ve ever felt that sudden wave of emotion in the middle of a grocery store, or found yourself revisiting old memories over a meal, you know how messy and real this journey can be. “Crying in H Mart” paints a picture of what it’s like to love deeply, lose someone you can’t imagine living without, and slowly find your way back to yourself.
So, here’s what you might want to carry with you: food isn’t just about nourishment—it’s a bridge. It can help you reconnect with memories, with your culture, and even with people you miss. Grief doesn’t follow a straight line; it moves at its own pace, and that’s okay. Creativity—whether that’s cooking, writing, or sharing your story—can gently turn pain into meaning and help you feel less alone. And don’t forget, rituals and community offer comfort, letting you know you’re held, even in your hardest moments.
Maybe most important of all, it’s those small, simple acts—making a favorite recipe, telling stories, or just sitting quietly with your feelings—that help keep your loved one’s spirit alive in everyday life.
If you’re finding your way through loss right now, know this: you don’t have to have everything figured out. Healing is messy. It’s more than okay to stumble, to take your time, and to let the rituals that matter to you bring comfort. The love you feel doesn’t fade with time or distance—it becomes a part of who you are. By honoring those you’ve lost, you’re also honoring yourself and helping build a world where memory and hope can exist side by side.
So, trust your own path. Let yourself move at the pace you need. And above all, remember—you are not alone on this journey.
